chapter_title: Fundamentals of Realtime Lighting in Unity
chapter_summary:
Welcome to the fascinating world of lighting in Unity! As a 3D artist, lighting is one of your most powerful tools for establishing mood, guiding player attention, and enhancing the realism of your scenes. We'll begin by exploring realtime lighting, which is dynamic and updates every frame, making it perfect for moving lights, characters, and dynamic environments. Realtime lights are computationally more expensive than baked lights, but they offer unparalleled flexibility and responsiveness.

Unity provides several fundamental light types, each serving a distinct purpose. The most common is the **Directional Light**, which simulates a distant light source like the sun. Its rays are parallel and extend infinitely across the scene, meaning its position doesn't matter, only its rotation. You'll typically have one primary directional light to define the overall illumination and shadow direction for your environment. Adjusting its rotation dramatically changes the time of day or the primary light source's angle, instantly altering the scene's mood. For instance, a low-angle directional light with an orange tint can evoke a sunset, while a high-angle, bright white light suggests midday.

Next, we have the **Point Light**, which emits light uniformly in all directions from a single point in space, much like a bare light bulb. Point lights are excellent for localized illumination, such as torches, lanterns, or magical orbs. Their key properties include **Range**, which defines how far the light reaches, and **Intensity**, controlling its brightness. A common mistake with point lights is setting their range too high, causing unnecessary light calculations across large areas, or too low, resulting in abrupt falloffs. Always consider the physical size and intended effect of your light source when setting its range and intensity.

The **Spot Light** is similar to a point light but emits light within a cone, like a flashlight or a car headlight. It has both a range and two cone angles: the **Spot Angle** (inner cone) and the **Penumbra Angle** (outer cone). Light within the inner cone is at full intensity, while it gradually fades out towards the outer cone. Spot lights are invaluable for creating focused illumination, highlighting specific objects, or simulating artificial light fixtures. When working with spot lights, pay close attention to the falloff between the inner and outer cones; a sharp falloff can look unnatural, while a gradual one can create a softer, more realistic effect.

Finally, while less commonly used for general scene illumination, **Area Lights** are crucial for realistic, soft lighting, especially in interior scenes. Unlike the other three types which are point-based, an Area Light emits light from a rectangular or disc-shaped surface. This results in much softer shadows and more diffuse lighting, mimicking light from windows, large studio lights, or emissive surfaces. Area lights are typically only supported by baked lighting or specific rendering pipelines (like HDRP) and are generally more performance-intensive in realtime. Understanding their purpose is key, even if your current project focuses on realtime directional, point, and spot lights.

When configuring any realtime light, several properties are universal. **Color** allows you to tint the light, which is fundamental for setting mood and atmosphere. A warm orange or yellow light feels inviting, while a cool blue or green light can feel eerie or sterile. **Intensity** controls the overall brightness. Be careful not to overexpose your scene with excessively high intensity values; often, subtle adjustments yield better results.

**Shadows** are arguably as important as the light itself. Realtime shadows add significant depth and realism to your scene, grounding objects within the environment. For each light that supports them (Directional, Point, Spot), you can enable shadows and choose their type (Hard, Soft, or None). **Hard Shadows** are sharp and pixelated, while **Soft Shadows** have a more natural, diffused edge. Unity's shadow settings, found under the Light component and in the Project Settings (Edit > Project Settings > Quality), allow you to control shadow resolution, distance, and other parameters. Higher resolution and longer distances mean better quality but also higher performance cost. A common mistake is using high-resolution shadows for distant objects where the detail isn't noticeable, leading to wasted performance. Always optimize shadow settings based on what's visible and impactful to the player.

For performance, it's critical to manage the number of realtime lights and their properties. Each realtime light that casts shadows adds significant rendering overhead. Consider using a few dominant realtime lights and supplementing with baked lighting or light probes (which we'll cover in upcoming chapters) for less critical light sources. The **Culling Mask** property on a light allows you to specify which layers of objects the light affects. This is a powerful optimization technique; for example, you might have a light only affecting the player character layer, or a spotlight only illuminating specific UI elements, preventing it from wasting calculations on the entire scene. Understanding and applying these fundamental concepts will lay a strong foundation for creating compelling and performant lighting in your Unity projects.

screens.title: Fundamentals of Realtime Lighting
screens.subtitle: How Directional, Point, Spot, and Area lights shape mood, visibility, and performance

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn what realtime lighting is, the four primary light types Unity provides, and why choosing the right light matters for both look and performance. Realtime lights update every frame, so they let you animate lights, attach lights to moving objects, and react to gameplay events. That flexibility comes at a cost: more realtime lights and realtime shadows increase rendering work and can reduce frame rates. You will see concrete examples: a directional light that simulates sun or moon, point lights that behave like bulbs, spot lights that act like flashlights, and area lights that create soft, diffuse illumination commonly used in interior scenes or high-fidelity pipelines. We'll also cover universal settings such as color, intensity, range, and cone angles, and show practical performance techniques like using culling masks to limit which layers a light affects. By the end of this chapter you'll know when to use each light type, how to tune its core properties for a specific mood, and how to balance visual fidelity with runtime cost. Think about a nighttime scene with a character and a distant moon: which lights would you choose and why?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Realtime lights are dynamic, frame-updated lights in Unity—useful for moving illumination but requiring careful tuning for performance.

screens.title: What is Realtime Lighting?
screens.subtitle: Definition, use cases, and the trade-off between flexibility and cost

narration.text: Realtime lighting refers to lights that are computed and updated every frame, which makes them suitable for any situation where light sources or illuminated objects move. Define it as dynamic illumination that responds immediately to animation, gameplay events, and moving cameras. A concrete example is a torch carried by a player: a realtime Point or Spot Light attached to the character moves with them and updates shadows each frame. The main benefit is flexibility: you can have lights that flicker, move, or react to spells and explosions. The main misconception is thinking realtime is always necessary; static scene elements often benefit from baked lighting, which precomputes illumination and is far cheaper at runtime. Another contrast is light probes and mixed lighting approaches: these let you retain dynamic objects while baking indirect lighting for static geometry. In practical terms, reserve realtime lights for sources that must change or influence dynamics. For all other sources, consider baking or light probes to preserve visual quality without the continuous C P U/G P U cost. As you proceed, ask yourself which lights in your scenes truly need to update every frame and which can be baked.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Realtime lights are dynamic lights calculated each frame—ideal for moving sources but more performance-costly than baked lighting.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › What is Realtime Lighting?
Definition

Realtime lighting explained

Computed every frame to support moving lights and dynamic scenes. Use when source or receiver movement matters.

Concrete example
A player carries a torch: attach a Point or Spot Light and let it update as the player moves. This keeps shadows and highlights aligned with the torch's position.
Common misconception
Believing all lights must be realtime. Many static lights are cheaper and look the same when baked.
Why it matters
Realtime lighting enables interaction and motion-driven effects but requires careful budgeting to avoid performance degradation.
Key Takeaway

Only use realtime lights where movement or interaction requires it; bake others for cheaper, stable lighting.

Contrast

Realtime vs Baked vs Probes

  • Realtime: dynamic, costly, per-frame updates.
  • Baked: precomputed, cheap at runtime, static only.
  • Light probes: blend baked indirect lighting for dynamic objects.
Pro tip
During iteration, reduce shadow resolution and shadow distance to speed up previewing changes.
Check your understanding
Name one light you would bake and one you would keep realtime in your current project, and explain why.

screens.title: Directional Light — The Sun and Moon
screens.subtitle: Parallel rays, rotation-driven illumination, and best practices

narration.text: A Directional Light simulates a distant light source, like the sun or moon. The defining characteristic is parallel rays: the light's position does not change the shadows or illumination, only its rotation matters. This makes it ideal for global illumination of outdoor scenes or any large-scale ambient source. A practical example is setting a Directional Light to simulate morning: rotate it to a low angle and tint it warm orange to create long, soft shadows and a sunset feel. A common misconception is trying to use multiple Directional Lights to simulate several sun sources; because rays are global and position-independent, multiple directional lights add confusing global illumination and can increase cost without realistic effect. Best practices include using a single primary directional light for your main sun or moon and tuning its intensity and color rather than stacking multiples. When shadows are enabled, directional shadows are powerful but also costly across large distances; adjust shadow distance and resolution in Quality settings to limit the performance hit. As you edit a scene, ask: does this light need to simulate a far-away source or a local fixture? If far-away, Directional is the correct choice.

keyIdea.title: Directional Light
keyIdea.text: Simulates distant, parallel light rays where rotation controls illumination direction and position is irrelevant.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Directional Light
Core Detail

Parallel rays and global illumination

Use when you need a single, scene-wide directional source like sun or moon. Rotation controls the light angle and shadows.

Concrete example
Rotate the directional light to X:45, Y:-30 to suggest morning; tint the color with a warm orange for sunrise feel.
Common mistake
Adding multiple directional lights to simulate several suns. Use additional point or spot lights for local sources instead.
Performance note
Directional shadows affect large areas; reduce shadow distance and resolution when distant detail isn't needed.
Key Takeaway

One directional light for the main sun/moon, tuned for rotation, color, and appropriate shadow distance.

Visual Comparison
Directional
Global, rotation-based, ideal for outdoor light across entire scene.
Point
Local, position dependent, best for bulbs or lanterns.
Spot
Cone-shaped; good for flashlights and focused highlights.
Try this
Rotate directional light through an angle range to preview how shadow length and scene mood change across day and night cycles.

screens.title: Point Light — Local, Omnidirectional Sources
screens.subtitle: Range, intensity, and common pitfalls when placing point lights

narration.text: A Point Light emits light uniformly in all directions from a single point, similar to a bare bulb. The two most important properties to configure are Range and Intensity. Range determines how far the light reaches; intensity controls brightness. A concrete scenario: place a point light a little above a lamp model, set range small enough to avoid illuminating distant walls, and choose an intensity that produces a visible warm pool without overexposing nearby materials. A frequent mistake is setting range too large, which expands the light's influence across the scene and increases lighting computations unnecessarily. Another error is using excessive intensity to force brightness instead of adjusting range or the object's material response. When shadows are enabled on a point light, remember that each shadow-casting light multiplies rendering work—so limit shadowed point lights to those that matter for composition or gameplay. The practical question to ask is whether this light needs to affect distant objects or just the immediate props. Keep range tight and intensity realistic to get the desired look with minimal performance cost. Point Light — Local, Omnidirectional Sources means emits light in all directions from a point; control with range and intensity and avoid overly large ranges that waste performance.. In practical terms, range, intensity, and common pitfalls when placing point lights. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Point Light
keyIdea.text: Emits light in all directions from a point; control with range and intensity and avoid overly large ranges that waste performance.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Point Light
Properties

Range and Intensity

Small range for localized pools, intensity to control perceived brightness. Tune both instead of pushing extreme values.

Example
Place a point light over a lamp model with Range 5 and Intensity 0.8 to create a believable nearby glow without lighting the whole room.
Common mistake
Large range values widen influence and increase per-frame calculations. Keep ranges focused on intended receivers.
Optimization tip
Disable shadows on minor point lights or restrict their culling mask to avoid unnecessary shadow passes.
Key Takeaway

Use point lights for local sources and keep range tight; disable shadows where they aren't visually important.

Scenario

Placing a lamp in a room

Set the point light slightly above the lamp's bulb, choose a warm color, set Range to cover nearby surfaces, and enable soft shadows only if the lamp's shadows are important to composition.

Check your understanding
Would you enable shadows for this lamp if players never see distant shadow edges? Explain briefly.
Pro tip
When iterating, temporarily disable shadow casting on point lights to speed up scene updates, then re-enable for final testing.

screens.title: Spot Light — Focused Beams and Penumbra
screens.subtitle: Inner cone, penumbra, and how to create natural falloff

narration.text: A Spot Light emits light within a cone and is ideal for flashlights, stage lights, or any focused highlight. Key properties are Range, Spot Angle (inner cone where light is fullest), and Penumbra Angle (outer cone where light fades). A clear example is a handheld flashlight: set a Spot Angle to define the focused beam, then increase the Penumbra Angle to soften the edge of the beam for realism. The common misconception is treating the Spot Angle alone as enough—without an appropriate penumbra the beam edge looks unnaturally hard. Another contrast is between Spot and Point lights: a spot is directional and confined to a cone, while a point light is omnidirectional. From a performance standpoint, spotlight shadows can be expensive when many are active and casting shadows across large ranges. Limit shadowed spotlights to key interactive elements, and prefer lower shadow resolutions for peripheral lights. As you tune a spotlight, consider whether the scene requires a crisp, theatrical edge or a softer, cinematic falloff and adjust angles and intensity accordingly. Spot Light — Focused Beams and Penumbra means cone-shaped light with inner and penumbra angles—useful for focused illumination and dramatic highlights.. In practical terms, inner cone, penumbra, and how to create natural falloff. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Spot Light
keyIdea.text: Cone-shaped light with inner and penumbra angles—useful for focused illumination and dramatic highlights.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Spot Light
Core Terms

Spot Angle and Penumbra

Spot Angle defines the core cone; Penumbra Angle defines the outer soft falloff. Balance both to avoid unnatural edges.

Concrete example
A flashlight can use Spot Angle 30 and Penumbra 55 for a focused beam with a soft edge that looks natural in motion.
Common misconception
Using a tiny Spot Angle with zero penumbra produces a harsh beam that rarely appears natural in real-world lighting.
Performance note
Spot lights that cast shadows have a per-light cost—prefer fewer shadowed spots or lower shadow resolution for ambient spots.
Key Takeaway

Use spotlights for directed beams and tune penumbra for natural falloff; restrict shadow casting to critical spots.

Placement Scenario

Flashlight on a character

Attach a spot light to the player's camera. Set moderate Spot Angle and larger Penumbra to avoid a hard-edged beam while keeping a clear central highlight for navigation.

Check your understanding
If the player complains about unrealistic beam edges, which property should you adjust first and why?
Pro tip
Animate Penumbra slightly to simulate a handheld torch wobble for added realism without heavy cost.

screens.title: Area Lights — Soft, Surface-Based Illumination
screens.subtitle: When to use area lights and their typical pipeline constraints

narration.text: Area Lights emit light from a surface rather than a point, producing softer shadows and more diffuse illumination that matches many real-world lighting scenarios like light through a window or large softboxes in a studio. In Unity, Area Lights are often limited to baked lighting workflows or specific high-fidelity pipelines; they are less commonly used for realtime in standard pipelines. A concrete use case is an interior scene where a large window should cast soft, broad light—baked area lights can produce realistic soft shadows across furniture with believable penumbra. A typical misconception is assuming area lights are interchangeable with point or spot lights; they are distinct because their source geometry affects shadow softness and the falloff area. If your project requires true realtime area lights, check whether your render pipeline supports them and be prepared for higher cost. For many real-time projects, simulate area-like softness by combining multiple spot lights with low intensity or using emissive geometry with baked indirect lighting. Always choose area lights when your pipeline and performance budget can support the richer, softer results they provide. Area Lights — Soft, Surface-Based Illumination means surface-based light producing soft shadows; commonly used in baked workflows or advanced render pipelines for realistic interior lighting.. In practical terms, when to use area lights and their typical pipeline constraints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Area Light
keyIdea.text: Surface-based light producing soft shadows; commonly used in baked workflows or advanced render pipelines for realistic interior lighting.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Area Lights
Purpose

Soft, surface-based illumination

Area lights mimic large emitters and produce diffuse, soft shadows ideal for interiors and studio lighting.

Concrete example
Use an area light to simulate sunlight through a wide window for softer, more realistic interior illumination when baking is acceptable.
Common misconception
Thinking area lights are the same as scaled point lights; they differ because their emitting surface alters shadow hardness and distribution.
Pipeline note
Area lights are typically baked or supported in HDRP; verify your render pipeline before relying on realtime area lights.
Key Takeaway

Prefer area lights for soft, high-fidelity interior lighting when your pipeline supports them; otherwise simulate with baked or emissive techniques.

Alternatives

Simulating area light effects

  • Baked area lights: high quality, static.
  • Emissive geometry: good for subtle ambient light when combined with probes.
  • Multiple low-intensity spots: approximate a soft, wide source in realtime with careful tuning.
Pro tip
If HDRP or baking isn't available, place emissive surfaces and bake indirect lighting to approximate area softness.

screens.title: Universal Light Properties: Color, Intensity, Range, Angle
screens.subtitle: How these settings affect mood, realism, and material response

narration.text: Every realtime light shares several fundamental properties: Color, Intensity, Range, and—when applicable—angles. Color tints the scene and is one of the fastest ways to set a mood: warm orange for sunset, cool blue for moonlight, or a greenish tint for an alien environment. Intensity controls brightness. A common mistake is overcompensating with intensity instead of adjusting exposure or material parameters; subtle intensity changes are often more believable than extremes. Range limits how far Point and Spot lights illuminate; keeping range focused reduces unnecessary per-frame calculations. Spot Angle and Penumbra Angle control how focused or soft cone lights appear—tight angles create theatrical highlights while wider angles wash areas softly. When tuning, look for visual scale: intensity and range should match the physical size and expected luminous power of the object you are simulating. For example, a small candle should have low intensity and short range; a streetlamp should be brighter and reach further. Use small iterative adjustments and compare with reference images to avoid unrealistic overexposure. Finally, test in the game's intended exposure setting: a light that looks correct at one exposure may be too bright or dim in another, so tune with the final camera settings in mind.

keyIdea.title: Core properties
keyIdea.text: Color, intensity, range, and angles govern visual mood and performance; tune them to match physical expectations and exposure settings.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Universal Light Properties
Process

Tuning workflow

  1. Set base color to convey time-of-day or mood.
  2. Adjust intensity to reach target brightness without clipping exposure.
  3. Set range to cover only intended receivers.
  4. For spotlights, tune inner and penumbra angles for realistic edges.
Concrete example
For a streetlamp, pick a warm color, set wider range and moderate intensity so nearby buildings are subtly lit, and enable soft shadows for ambience.
Misconception
Turning intensity up to compensate for poor range yields unrealistic falloff. Fix range first, then fine-tune intensity.
Key Takeaway

Tune properties in order: color, range, intensity, and angles; match the light's physical scale for believable results.

Cards
Color
Sets mood and temperature. Warm colors feel inviting; cool colors feel distant or eerie.
Intensity
Brightness control; avoid overexposure by checking camera exposure settings.
Range & Angles
Define where light reaches and how focused cone lights appear.

screens.title: Realtime Shadows — Hard vs Soft and Quality Settings
screens.subtitle: Choosing shadow types, resolution, and distance for the right balance

narration.text: Shadows establish depth and anchor objects to the environment. In Unity realtime lights support Hard and Soft shadows. Hard shadows produce crisp edges and are cheaper, while Soft shadows produce gradual edges that look more natural but cost more to compute. Important settings include shadow resolution and shadow distance in Project Settings > Quality. Shadow resolution dictates the texel density of shadow maps; higher resolution yields crisper shadows but increases memory and rendering cost. Shadow distance controls how far from the camera shadows are rendered; reducing this value prevents distant objects from wasting shadowing cycles. A common mistake is enabling high-resolution shadows across the entire scene, even for distant, low-impact objects. Instead, reserve high resolution for close-up areas and set a reasonable shadow distance. Another optimization is limiting which lights cast shadows—use culling masks or disable shadow casting on lights that only contribute subtle fill. Concrete example: in a scene with a character and decorative lamps, let the primary directional light cast soft shadows with medium resolution, enable shadows on the player's flashlight only if its shadows affect navigation, and disable shadows on small ambient point lights to save cost. What shadows truly affect player perception in your scene?

keyIdea.title: Realtime Shadows
keyIdea.text: Shadows add realism but cost performance; choose hard or soft, adjust resolution and distance, and limit shadow casters to what matters.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Realtime Shadows
Key Choices

Hard vs Soft

Hard shadows are crisp and less costly; soft shadows are natural but more expensive. Choose based on visual priority and budget.

Project settings
Adjust Shadow Resolution and Shadow Distance under Quality to limit cost for distant shadows.
Concrete example
Enable soft shadows for the main directional light and disable shadow casting on minor decorative lights to reduce render passes.
Common mistake
Using unnecessarily high shadow resolution for distant objects where the detail is not visible.
Key Takeaway

Optimize shadows by limiting shadow-casting lights, lowering distant resolution, and using soft shadows where value is high.

Quick checklist
  • Are shadows visible to the player? If not, disable shadow casting.
  • Is shadow distance tuned to camera range?
  • Use higher resolution only for close-up critical shadows.
Pro tip
When profiling, toggle shadow options to measure which setting produces the largest performance change and prioritize adjustments there.

screens.title: Performance Strategies for Realtime Lighting
screens.subtitle: Balancing quality and frame rate with selective realtime usage

narration.text: Realtime lights are powerful but expensive. The guiding principle is to use the fewest realtime lights necessary and to make each one matter visually or functionally. One primary technique is selective shadowing: only let lights cast shadows when those shadows impact player perception or gameplay. Another technique is culling masks, which tell a light which object layers it should affect; for instance, you can have a light only affect the player layer, reducing unnecessary lighting on world geometry. Also, keep light ranges tight and intensities realistic to limit the number of affected fragments. Use baked lighting for static elements and light probes to provide baked indirect lighting for dynamic objects. A practical example: in a scene with many local lamps, keep only one or two lamps casting realtime shadows near the player and bake the rest or use emissive textures for subtle fill. Common misconceptions include thinking shadow type swaps (hard vs soft) will solve all issues; while helpful, true savings come from reducing the number of shadow-casting lights and restricting their influence with culling masks. Conclude each optimization pass by profiling the scene to verify visual impact versus performance gain.

keyIdea.title: Performance principle
keyIdea.text: Minimize active realtime lights and shadow casters; use culling masks and baking where possible to preserve frame rate.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Performance Strategies
Checklist

Optimize realtime lighting

  • Use culling masks to limit a light's affected layers.
  • Disable shadows for non-critical lights.
  • Bake static lighting and use probes for dynamic objects.
Concrete example
In a room with many lamps, allow only nearby lamps to cast realtime shadows; bake the rest to preserve fidelity at lower runtime cost.
Key Takeaway

Profile first, then apply culling masks and shadow limits to the lights that most affect performance while retaining visual priorities.

Optimization cards
Culling Mask
Assign layers to a light so it only affects essential objects, like the player or specific scene elements.
Shadow Casters
Mark only the lights that need to cast shadows; disable casting on decorative lights.
Bake vs Realtime
Bake static sources and reserve realtime lights for moving elements to reduce per-frame load.

screens.title: Hands-on: Dynamic Scene Lighting Setup
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step guide to building the sample scene and tuning lights

narration.text: Let's walk through the hands-on activity step by step so you can reproduce and verify results in Unity. First, create a new 3D scene and add a Plane for the ground, plus a few Cube and Sphere objects at varying heights to act as props. This provides visible geometry to observe lighting and shadows. Second, locate the default Directional Light, rotate it to simulate morning—try X:45, Y:-30—and set its color to a warm orange and intensity around 1.2. Enable Soft Shadows to observe gentle shadow edges. Third, add a Point Light near one cube: position it slightly above the object, set color to a soft blue, intensity to about 0.8, range to 5, and enable soft shadows only if required for composition. Fourth, add a Spot Light pointing down at another sphere: set range to 8, Spot Angle to 45, Penumbra to 60, intensity around 1.0, and enable soft shadows. Finally, experiment with Edit > Project Settings > Quality to change shadow resolution and distance; observe how higher resolution improves close shadows but increases cost. Test culling masks on your lights by placing props on separate layers and letting lights affect only relevant layers. After you finish, reflect: which changes had the largest visual effect and which most impacted performance?

screens.title: Common Questions & Misconceptions
screens.subtitle: Multiple-choice reasoning and practical debugging tips

narration.text: Let's review common questions learners encounter and how to reason about them. Question one: for a flashlight and a distant moon, which lights are appropriate? The correct answer is a Spot Light for the flashlight and a Directional Light for the moon. That matches their physical distributions: focused cone versus far-away parallel rays. Another frequent issue is performance drops when many realtime point lights are active. A primary optimization is culling masks: restrict lights to layers of objects they must affect rather than increasing their range or changing color. A misconception is that changing color or shadow hardness alone will eliminate performance cost; while helpful, these changes don't reduce the number of lighting calculations like culling masks do. For debugging, toggle shadow casting per light to see which lights contribute the most draw calls, and use Unity's Profiler to measure the cost of shadow map passes. Finally, when a scene looks washed out after adding many lights, consider lowering intensity values and relying on baked indirect lighting for ambient fill. Which debugging step will you perform first in your own scene, and why?

Common questions & quick answers

Q: Flashlight & moon
Answer: Spot Light for flashlight, Directional Light for moon. Spot for cone, directional for distant parallel rays.
Q: Many point lights cause lag
Answer: Use culling masks, tighten ranges, and reduce shadow casters rather than increasing ranges or just swapping shadow type.
Debug tip
Toggle shadow casting per light and profile frame time to identify the costly lights to optimize first.
Design check
If the scene is visually washed out, reduce light intensities and rely on baked indirect light for ambient energy.

Which optimization will you try first in your project: culling masks, disabling shadows, or baking static lights? Why?

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember about realtime lighting

narration.text: Let's summarize the core concepts you should remember. Directional lights simulate distant sources with parallel rays; rotation matters more than position. Point lights are omnidirectional, useful for local lamps and require careful range and intensity settings. Spot lights create cones with inner and penumbra angles—use penumbra to soften edges for realism. Area lights emit from surfaces and produce soft illumination, but are typically used with baked lighting or advanced pipelines. Realtime shadows add depth but come at a performance cost; choose hard or soft depending on priority, and tune resolution and distance. Finally, performance techniques such as culling masks, limiting shadow casters, and baking static lights are essential to balance fidelity and frame rate. Keep these principles in mind as practical rules of thumb when building scenes: use realtime sparingly, tune properties to physical scale, and profile to guide optimizations. screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three core reminders for practical lighting work

narration.text: Keep these three compact reminders at hand as you light scenes. First: choose light type by behavior—Directional for distant sources, Point for local bulbs, Spot for cones, Area for surface-based softness when supported. Second: tune properties in order—color for mood, range and angles for spatial influence, then intensity for perceived brightness—this sequence helps avoid unrealistic settings. Third: optimize early—limit shadow-casting lights, use culling masks to reduce affected objects, and bake static contributions where possible. These three rules quickly improve both the visual outcome and runtime performance of your scenes. As a final reflection, think about your next scene: which light will you convert from realtime to baked or restrict with a culling mask to improve performance? This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
